name: Duchenne smile

lead: A Duchenne smile combines the zygomatic major, which lifts the corners of the mouth, with the orbicularis oculi, which raises the cheeks and creates crow's feet. It is named for the nineteenth-century French neurologist Guillaume Duchenne, who described two kinds of smile.

A meta-analysis found that Duchenne smiles and the people showing them are rated as more authentic, genuine, attractive and trustworthy than non-Duchenne smiles. That is why looksmaxxing forum members recommend a natural smile over a forced closed-mouth one, and why photo-rating tests are used to compare them.

paras: People practise smiling in a mirror, aim to recall genuinely pleasant thoughts so the eyes engage, and compare photos. Forum posters report testing smile types on photo-rating sites. Research on facial feedback has used held-in-mouth tools such as chopsticks to produce smile shapes in the lab.

There are no physical risks from smiling. Researchers note that smile perception varies by culture, and that eye wrinkle treatments that paralyse the muscles around the eyes can prevent a Duchenne smile.

angle.text: The Duchenne smile changes expression rather than structure: the eyes participate in the smile, and observers rate it as more genuine and attractive in the meta-analytic literature.

lead: A Duchenne smile is a smile that uses both the zygomatic major muscle, which pulls the lip corners up, and the orbicularis oculi muscle around the eyes, which lifts the cheeks and narrows the eyes [1][2]. A smile using only the mouth is called non-Duchenne. Paul Ekman and colleagues published a 1990 paper on the brain physiology of the Duchenne smile [3].

In looksmaxxing discussion, the Duchenne smile is presented as a free way to look more attractive in photos and in person. A looksmax.org poster says the closed-mouth forced smile of some members scores lower on photo-rating than a proper smile [4].
A 2016 meta-analysis found Duchenne smiles and their owners were rated more positively on authenticity, genuineness, attractiveness and trustworthiness [2].

paras: Guillaume Duchenne, a French neurologist, studied facial expressions in the mid-nineteenth century and distinguished two kinds of smile [1]. The orbicularis oculi component raises the cheeks and produces crow's feet. The smile has been described informally as smiling with the eyes [1]. A voluntary mouth-only smile is sometimes called a Pan Am smile [1].

A looksmax.org thread argues that men should smile and that a genuine smile beats a neutral or forced one, citing improved scores on a photo-rating tool [4]. The poster contrasts this with advice that men should avoid smiling to look more dominant [4].

The 2016 meta-analysis found larger differences when stimuli were videos, when smiles were elicited naturally rather than posed, and when Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles were not matched for lip-corner intensity [2]. Later reviews have examined whether eye constriction reliably signals positive emotion and have argued the evidence concerns what smiles do to observers as much as what they express [5][6][7].

Facial feedback research tests whether adopting a smile changes mood or stress. In a 2012 experiment, participants holding chopsticks in a smile shape had lower heart rates during stress recovery than neutral-expression participants, with a slight advantage for Duchenne smiles [8]. A 2002 study found Duchenne smilers reported more positive experience to pleasant clips [9]. A 2021 needle-injection trial examined smiling versus grimacing [10].

Wikipedia notes that smiling norms vary: a large cross-cultural study found smiling people were seen as less intelligent in some cultures, and that too much smiling can read as shallow or dishonest [1]. The broader facial feedback hypothesis has a mixed record: a 2016 multi-lab replication did not reproduce the 1988 pen study, while a 2019 meta-analysis found small but robust effects [11].

The 2016 meta-analysis of perception studies found Duchenne smiles rated as more authentic, attractive and trustworthy [2]. Experimental studies of manipulated smiles reported lower heart rate in stress recovery [8] and more positive reported experience to pleasant films [9]. A 2020 study reported an association between Duchenne smile and quality of life and survival in hemodialysis patients [12]. In facial reanimation surgery, multivector gracilis flaps are used to restore smile after facial paralysis [13].
